CHAPTER 6 
LIMITS ON THE BARGAIN AND ITS PERFORMANCE 
Unconscionability: 
Arbitration Clauses 
Cases concerning the enforceability of mandatory arbitration clauses 
have generatl d some of the most contested rulings in contemporary 
contract law These clauses are common in employment contracts, often 
imposed as n condition of employment, and in consumer contracts. As 
discussed in Chapter 1, pp. 46-4 7, arbitration as an alternative to 
litigation ha!- taken on increasing importance over the last few decades. 
Some of the reasons behind this trend are clear. Many parties choose to 
arbitrate m order to avoid or lower the costs-in 
time, in money, in 
publicity--of seeking a remedy in court. But what if an arbitration clause 
is not so mud. chosen as imposed as part of the boilerplate in a standard 
form or adhel:!i\e contract? 
This qul' t1on comes up often in the context of employment contracts. 
For a basel m answer, one can look to an important 2001 Supreme Court

agreement; ell e generally enforceable under the Federal Arbitration Act 
(FAA), "save for upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity for the 
revocation of ·my contract." Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams, 532 U.S. 
105, 112 (2001) The doctrine of unconscionability, of course, is one such 
ground for revoking a contract. 
Yet consensus on the standard for 
invoking thl J,)ctrine remains elusive.

Court in

of the
